title: Faraday's Laws
notes: Faraday's first observation is that an emf appears in a circuit when the magnetic flux through it is changing. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing.
The flux through one turn is Φ = B A when the field is uniform and perpendicular to the area. At an angle, the perpendicular component B cosθ is used. Flux linkage for N turns is NΦ.
Faraday's law says the induced emf equals the negative of the rate of change of flux linkage. A faster change means a larger emf.
The flux can be changed by changing the field, by changing the area of the loop, or by rotating the loop. A generator rotates a coil so that the angle changes continuously.
The minus sign is Lenz's law. The induced current makes a field that opposes the change in flux that caused it.
If the circuit is open there is still an induced emf, but no induced current. Current needs a closed path.
confusion: ❌ 'Induced EMF depends only on magnetic field strength.' ✅ It depends on the *rate of change* of magnetic flux (dΦ/dt). A strong field that doesn't change induces no EMF.
❌ 'Faraday's law applies only to closed circuits.' ✅ The *law* defines the EMF induced in a loop; a physical current flows only if the circuit is *closed*.
❌ 'More turns always mean more flux.' ✅ More turns increase the *total flux linkage* (NΦ), which proportionally increases the induced EMF.
A steady field does not induce an emf.
Emf depends on the rate, not on the flux alone.
An open circuit can have an emf and no current.
Area, field and angle are three different ways to change the flux.

exercises.question: A single loop of area 0.040 m^2 is perpendicular to a field that rises by 0.50 T in 0.20 s. Find the magnitude of the induced emf.
steps: The area vector stays perpendicular, so ΔΦ = A ΔB.
One turn, so the linkage rate is the same number.
The direction of the induced current would oppose the rise in field.
